sec.title: Background
sec.p: This study aims to report a case of pulmonary epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (PEH) achieving pathological complete remission following neoadjuvant treatment, thereby enhancing clinical understanding of this rare disease and providing valuable treatment insights.

sec.title: Case presentation
sec.p: The patient’s imaging examination revealed a single large tumor on one side of the lung with lymph node metastasis. After treatment with albumin paclitaxel + carboplatin + bevacizumab, the tumor disappeared from the imaging findings, and postoperative pathology confirmed that the patient achieved pathological complete remission.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: PEH is rare in clinical practice and is a type of malignant tumor without characteristic clinical manifestations, and the diagnosis relies on pathological and immunohistochemical examinations. Single or few lesions can be treated surgically, whereas those that cannot undergo surgery can be treated with chemotherapy and targeted therapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (EHE) is a rare tumor that originates from vascular endothelial cells [1]. Studies have reported that its incidence is less than one in a million [2]. It was originally described as intravascular bronchioloalveolar tumor (IVBAT) by Dail and Liebow in 1975 [3]. In 1982, Weiss and Enzinger renamed IVBAT EHE [4]. EHE is a malignant vascular tumor with moderate to low differentiation characteristics and some degree of metastatic ability [5], and its degree of malignancy is between that of completely benign hemangiomas and highly malignant angiosarcomas [4]. Women account for a greater proportion, with some statistics showing a ratio of approximately 1:4 between men and women [6]. However, the incidence is lower in children and elderly individuals [7]. It is commonly found in bones, blood vessels, head, and liver and kidneys, with EHE occurring in lung tissue being called pulmonary epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (PEH), which is a very rare site of occurrence [8]. Currently, there is no guideline-recommended standard treatment program for PEH, and the literature reports are extremely limited. Current domestic and international reports are dominated by case reports and small sample reports. We searched for relevant literature domestically and internationally, thus far, only a few hundred cases have been reported worldwide, to the best of our knowledge, there appear to be no reported cases of pathological complete remission after neoadjuvant therapy. This article reports one case of PEH that was confirmed by pathology at our hospital and achieved pathological complete remission after neoadjuvant treatment. Moreover, we summarize its clinical manifestations, imaging manifestations, pathological features, treatment and prognosis by combining the relevant domestic and international literature. The literature is as follows.

sec.title: Case report
sec.p: The patient, a 66-year-old male, was admitted to the hospital on February 17, 2022, for “cough for 1 week”, and a chest CT revealed a soft tissue mass in the upper lobe of the right lung, with compression of adjacent organs. The lesion was approximately 5.0 cm×5.5 cm in extent, the mediastinal window revealed enlarged subcarinal lymph nodes and enlarged hilar lymph nodes, and there was no fluid accumulation in the bilateral pleural cavity (Fig. 1). After multidisciplinary discussion, neoadjuvant treatment was selected. CT-guided lung puncture biopsy was performed, and pathology and immunohistochemistry revealed epithelioid hemangioendothelioma (Figs. 2a and 2b). The immunohistochemistry results were as follows: CD31 (+), ERG (partially +), Ki-67 (index 20%), CK7 (-), TTF-1 (-), NapsinA (-), P63 (-), P40 (-), CK (-), CK8/18 (-), and SMA (-). The genetic test result was positive for the WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion gene. The patient was given 4 cycles of paclitaxel + carboplatin chemotherapy and 3 cycles of bevacizumab, and a repeat chest CT on June 28, 2022, revealed a patchy hyperdense shadow in the upper lobe of the right lung with exudative changes around the lesion (Fig. 3). After another multidisciplinary consultation, thoracoscopic right upper lobectomy + mediastinal lymph node dissection was performed on July 3, 2022. Postoperative pathology revealed partial subpleural and interstitial fibrotic tissue proliferation, congestion of alveolar spaces with hemorrhage, intraluminal deposition of fibrinous material, local bronchial dilation, vascular proliferation, thickening of the vessel wall, and chronic inflammatory cell infiltration (Figs. 4a and 4b). No tumor was observed at the cut edge of the bronchus. No tumor was detected in lymph nodes of all regions: Parabronchial lymph nodes (0/3), paratracheal lymph nodes (0/1), subcarinal lymph nodes (0/3), paraesophageal lymph nodes (0/1), lymph nodes of the lower lung ligament (0/1), hilar lymph nodes (0/3), perihilar lymph nodes (0/6). The patient underwent regular follow-up after surgery. The chest CT in April 2023 revealed no obvious abnormal density shadows around the surgical area, no lesions in the hilar region, and no obvious enlarged lymph nodes in the mediastinum. The chest CT in April 2024 revealed no lesions in the right lung (Fig. 5). The patient had no tumor in the mediastinum. There were no abnormalities in the brain or abdomen on related examinations.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: It is currently believed that EHE is a borderline and malignant-trending tumor, and it is rarer and more aggressive in the lungs than in other sites.

sec.title: Clinical features
sec.p: The incidence rate of EHE is less than one in a million, among which the probability of isolated lung involvement is 12% [6]. PEH is more common in women, with a prevalence of up to 80% [9]. Although it is more common in women, the symptoms are more severe in men than in women. EHE can occur in all age groups, with half of the patients being under 40 years old [10]. PEH lacks characteristic clinical manifestations, with approximately half of the patients having only mild symptoms or no symptoms at all [11], such as chest pain and cough, and severe cases may experience dyspnea. Some patients may have symptoms such as anemia, pain, weight loss, and fatigue. In our case, the patient experienced cough, which was caused by a tumor invading the trachea, as observed via CT. Lymph node involvement is common in PEH [8], and our patient presented with lymph node metastasis on CT. The liver, bones, and brain are also common sites of metastasis. PEH often presents with multiple lesions in the lung and, in many cases, is of multicentric origin rather than intrapulmonary metastasis. Amin et al. [12] reported that 50.5% of PEH patients had metastasis, with local metastasis to the pleura at 20.4% and lymph node metastasis at 10.8%. Male sex, multiple bilateral lung lesions, symptoms of chest pain, cough, hemoptysis, pleural effusion, distant metastasis, and lymph node metastasis are important risk factors that often suggest a poor prognosis for patients with lung EHE.

sec.title: Imaging features
sec.p: PEH has no specific imaging features, and typical chest CT scans of PEH patients often reveal multiple small nodules with a diameter of less than 2 cm along the pulmonary vasculature in both lungs [13, 14]. The diagnosis is based on pathological and immunohistochemical examinations. Some patients may present with solitary nodules, with a reported incidence of 21.4% by a Japanese scholar [15], while others may present as solitary solid masses resembling lung cancer [16]. Some patients may present with enlarged hilar or mediastinal lymph nodes [14] and a poor prognosis with an increased risk of progression when there is pleural thickening or pleural effusion [17]. Several studies have reported that 18 F-FDG-PET/CT can be helpful in diagnosing PEH [10, 13, 17], with low to moderate activity on 18 F-FDG-PET/CT in PEH [18], but high uptake has also been reported in aggressive PEH [10, 19].

sec.title: Pathological features
sec.p: Since PEH lacks characteristic clinical manifestations and specific imaging findings and has no specific laboratory markers, diagnosis depends on pathology and immunohistochemistry. The main methods for obtaining pathological samples are percutaneous lung biopsy or surgical resection. The histopathological features of PEH are epithelioid endothelial cells arranged in cords, strands, or glandular patterns, with varying degrees of vacuoles in the cytoplasm of the tumor cells. Occasionally, the cells are compressed into an impression ring [20], with the nucleus displaying pleomorphism, and may contain intracytoplasmic vacuoles and alterations in the extracellular matrix [21]. The central area of the nodule has fewer tumor cells, whereas the peripheral area has relatively more tumor cells. The tumor cells can spread through small blood vessels within the alveolar septa to surrounding tissues, and the tumor tissue can invade pulmonary arteries and veins, nerves, and lymphatic tissue. Necrotic tissue and calcification can be observed in the tumor, and follicular epithelial hyperplasia can be observed around the tumor, often with inflammatory cell infiltration.

The immunohistochemical expression of various vascular endothelial cell antigens can be helpful in the diagnosis of EHE. Common antigens include platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1 (CD31), cell surface glycoprotein (CD34), factor VIII-related antigen, Fli-1 (Friend leukemia integration 1 transcription factor), and erythroblast transformation-specific related gene (ERG) [21, 22]. CD34 is expressed in more than 90% of vascular tumors and has low specificity in the diagnosis of EHE, whereas CD31 is considered a relatively specific vascular tumor marker [23]. ERG, which is expressed in vascular endothelial cells, is an erythroblast transformation-specific (ETS) family transcription factor, and Anderson et al. [21] reported that the positive expression rates of CD31 and ERG in 52 cases of thoracic epithelioid vascular tumors were 96% and 100%, respectively. Therefore, ERG can be used as a new marker for benign and malignant vascular tumors with high specificity. Currently, a combination of CD31, CD34, and ERG is recommended as the first-line antibody for the diagnosis of EHE. The immunohistochemical antigenic expression of CD31 and ERG was positive in the case we reported, which is in accordance with the antigenic expression reported in the previous literature and Anderson’s study.

According to studies, approximately 90% of EHE cases harbor the WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion gene, and 10% possess the YAP1-TFE3 fusion gene [21]. We conducted genetic testing, and the results revealed the presence of the WWTR1-CAMTA1 fusion gene, which further provides strong confirmation of the diagnosis.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: Because the incidence of PEH is relatively rare, the current domestic and international reports are mostly based on case reports and lack large-scale clinical trials, so there is no standard treatment plan. However, by summarizing the relevant articles published at home and abroad, the following conclusions can be drawn: 1.If the lesion is solitary or there are a fewer lesions, surgical resection should be the first choice. In our case, lung lobectomy was performed to completely remove the tumor, but most of the patients did not have the opportunity for surgery because most of the PEHs presented with bilateral multifocal lesions. Some studies have shown that in patients who have the opportunity for surgery, extended resection does not improve the long-term survival of patients compared with wedge resection, which has the same survival as extended resection [24]. However, lung lobectomy is helpful in staging the tumor because of better lymph node clearance, and the importance of lymph node clearance may gradually increase with increasing reports of the disease. The survival time is generally longer in patients who are able to undergo surgical treatment [25]. 2. For patients who cannot undergo surgery, chemotherapy has become the basic treatment option. Currently, there is no unified chemotherapy plan, and its efficacy is uncertain. The current reported options include paclitaxel, carboplatin, adriamycin, and gemcitabine, among others, of which paclitaxel combined with carboplatin is the most commonly used chemotherapy plan at present [26]. 3.Targeted therapy: Because PEH originates from the endothelium, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) are both expressed in PEH tumor cells. VEGF and VEGFR are closely related to the proliferation and metastasis of tumors, so antiangiogenic drugs may be a viable option for the treatment of metastatic PEH. Studies have shown that bevacizumab combined with carboplatin and paclitaxel is effective in treating PEH [27]. Ye et al. [28] reported one case of a PEH patient who experienced a gradual reduction in chest pain and stable disease for 8 months after receiving bevacizumab combined with carboplatin and paclitaxel chemotherapy for 6 cycles. Shiba et al. [8] reported that, for both bevacizumab combined with carboplatin and paclitaxel or bevacizumab combined with carboplatin and pemetrexed in the treatment of PEH, the patient’s condition could achieve partial remission. However, the effects were mostly partial remission, and we have not seen reports of pathological complete remission. The case we reported achieved complete remission from both imaging and pathological perspectives, which can provide some guidance for relevant treatment plans in the future. Recombinant human endostatin injection can inhibit the migration of endothelial cells that form blood vessels, which can inhibit tumor neovascularization, and Ye reported that the treatment plan of recombinant human endostatin injection combined with paclitaxel/carboplatin improved the clinical condition and stabilized the disease [28]. Anlotinib is a novel small-molecule multitarget tyrosine kinase inhibitor that can effectively inhibit VEGFR and antitumor angiogenesis and inhibit tumor growth. In addition, thalidomide [29], apatinib [26] and other drugs have also achieved good results in small samples or case reports, but the current sample size is small, and more clinical studies are needed to confirm the results. 4.Radiation therapy: PEH has only a low to moderate sensitivity to radiation therapy, with poor effects [30].

This study has several limitations. First, as a single-case report, studies with larger sample sizes are required to validate the efficacy of this treatment regimen. Furthermore, although the patient has achieved nearly two years of disease-free survival, the follow-up duration remains relatively short for evaluating the long-term efficacy and survival rate of PEH, and longer-term monitoring data are needed.

In summary, PEH is a rare low-to-moderate malignant vascular endothelial cell-derived tumor with a low incidence and few reported cases in the literature but high potential harm. It should therefore be given greater attention by clinicians, as its clinical manifestations and imaging examinations lack specificity, making it very easy for it to be misdiagnosed clinically. The confirmation of the diagnosis needs to be based on the results of pathological examinations and immunohistochemistry. Patients with symptoms or metastasis have a poor prognosis. In terms of treatment, in addition to surgery, there is currently no standard treatment plan or guideline. Chemotherapy is the most frequently used treatment plan at present, as PEH originates from the vascular endothelium, and antiangiogenic drugs are expected to achieve very good results. With the increasing number of clinical reports, it is hoped that a rational standard comprehensive treatment plan can be provided for the treatment of this disease.

notes.title: Author contributions
notes.p: Xin Feng designed the study protocol, collected and organized clinical data of the patient, and drafted the initial manuscript. Fei Chen performed systematic literature retrieval and in-depth analysis, summarized relevant research progress, and revised the manuscript for academic accuracy. Ying Wang formulated the neoadjuvant treatment plan, monitored the patient’s treatment response, and supplemented clinical outcome data. Xiaomei Li provided pathological sections, conducted immunohistochemical staining analysis, and interpreted pathological results. Huayu Zhao assisted in surgical planning, collected intraoperative data, and organized imaging materials (Figs. 1, 2a, 2b, 3, 4a, 4b and 5). Wenming Xiao supervised the entire study, coordinated multidisciplinary collaboration, revised the final manuscript, and is responsible for the integrity of the data. All authors read and approved the final manuscript.
